paras: The killing of Antonio Maria Baca was the fatal shooting of a prisoner held by an armed citizens' committee of safety at Socorro, New Mexico Territory, on the night of December 28-29, 1880. The committee had seized Baca as a hostage and named him as one of the men wanted for the murder of A. M. Conkling, editor of the Socorro Sun, and a guard shot him dead after, by the guards' account, he fired a revolver and wounded another guard. Papers carried the shooting as part of a feared armed conflict between the "Americans" of Socorro and a "powerful and numerous Mexican family."

After Conkling's murder, residents led by Col. E. W. Eaton organized a committee of safety, and forty-three men signed a pledge to avenge the killing and preserve "good order." According to the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, Sheriff Garcia evaded the committee's demand that he serve murder warrants on three Baca brothers, first asking for the warrants in Spanish and then shutting his door on the party.

In the early hours of the next morning, armed committee members forced the sheriff and his deputy, Felipe Baca, to come with them and marched on the Baca family house at Cuba, a village about a mile and a half below Socorro. When Eaton threatened to blow up the house with giant powder, which the Gazette admitted had not been placed, twelve men and boys surrendered, and the committee kept five of them as hostages until the murderers should be produced. The hostages were the sheriff, the deputy, Antonio Maria Baca, former probate judge Dionicio Jaramillo and Estevan Baca, and they were held under guard in a wine room while patrols watched the town.

A committee of Mexican residents negotiated bonds for the hostages, but as they were about to be freed the committee decided that Antonio Maria Baca, not the "Mesices Baca" named in the coroner's verdict, was the man wanted and refused to release him on any bail. That night guards heard noises in the room and suspected an attempt to dig out, and as Dr. Dobbins and Jack Thatcher entered, Baca fired at Thatcher. Baca was shot through the head and killed instantly, while Thatcher was wounded in the left breast by a small No. 22 revolver whose source the Gazette called a mystery.

On December 29 Judge Parks of the Second Judicial District released the remaining prisoners from the citizens' custody on heavy bail. Federal infantry arrived to guard the post office and railway property, identified by the Gazette as Company G of the 18th Infantry and by the Santa Fe dispatch as a company of the Thirteenth. No report of an inquest into Baca's death, or of any charge against his guards, appears in the coverage.

The Las Vegas Morning Gazette sent a correspondent to Socorro and printed the fullest account under the headline "A War of Races Barely Averted by the Determined Men of Socorro," written from the committee's headquarters at the Park House. The paper said Socorro had been "horribly maligned" by reports of American violence, blamed a telegraph operator for the rumor that five Mexicans had been lynched, and called the wounded guard "a brave fellow and universally liked."

The Santa Fe wire dispatch, which like the Gazette's story came from the committee's side, ran on December 30 and 31 in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Phoenix Herald and was condensed in early January in weekly news columns in Minnesota, Tennessee and Ohio. These reports gave the killing a single sentence, describing Baca only as "one of the prisoners held by the citizens," and the weeklies garbled his name as Antoine M. Boca, Antoine M. Baca or Jose M. Boca. An earlier Santa Fe dispatch in the Gold Hill Daily News called the town's Mexican residents "Greasers," and a Cheyenne dispatch named the accused assassin as "Jacob Baca."

The papers did not agree on who was accused of killing Conkling. The Gazette said the coroner's jury had named "Mesices Baca" and that Antonio Maria Baca was singled out only as the hostages were about to be released, while the Gold Hill dispatch called the prisoner the man "who recently killed Conkling."

reader.title: Killing of Antonio Maria Baca
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A guard of an armed citizens' committee of safety shot dead a prisoner the committee had seized as a hostage from a family it called 'Mexican', after, by the committee's account, the prisoner fired on the guards (A2, A3, A4); the target was not reported as Black.

Baca was killed while held without lawful authority by a committee of more than forty men formed to avenge Conkling's murder (A2, A3, A4), but every account says a single guard shot him after he fired and wounded another guard (A3, A4), and no other version appears, so whether the killing was an execution under a pretext of justice or a shooting in an exchange of fire cannot be settled from these papers.

The Las Vegas Gazette's on-the-scene report (A3) and the separate Santa Fe wire dispatch (A4, reprinted in A7-A10) agree that Baca, a prisoner of the citizens, shot a guard and was killed by another guard, though both versions come from the committee's side.
